analysis.one_liner: Directs Treasury to study having the IRS send taxpayers pre-filled tax returns to review and sign.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Department to report within a year on what it would take for the IRS to offer taxpayers an optional return that is already filled out with wage and income information the government already receives. Taxpayers could check it, change it, or ignore it and file their own way. The bill itself did not create return-free filing; it set a goal of 2022 and ordered a study of the costs and legal barriers.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had advanced toward actual return-free filing, tens of millions of taxpayers with simple finances — wages, a standard deduction — would save the hours spent preparing returns and the money spent on paid preparers or software, which typically runs a few hundred dollars for an in-person preparation. The bill as written would only have produced a government study, so its immediate benefit was limited to building the record for that change.

how_it_helps.text: Expresses the sense of Congress that the IRS should begin offering pre-prepared returns to as many taxpayers as possible by tax year 2022.

Requires the Treasury Secretary, in consultation with the Taxpayer Advocate Service, to report within one year on the steps needed — earlier W-2 deadlines, faster information processing, secure online IRS accounts — and to analyze the budget, administrative, and legislative barriers, including required appropriations.
Would have taxpayers keep the option to download their information for use in private tax software, rather than forcing anyone into a single government filing channel.

analysis.who_pays: Tax preparation and tax software companies would lose revenue if pre-filled IRS returns became available, since millions of filers with simple returns would no longer need their products or services. The IRS would also need appropriations to build and operate the system, which the mandated study was designed to estimate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Paid tax preparers and software companies

drawbacks.text: The bill as written changes nothing on its own: it sets a goal and orders a study, so even full enactment would not have delivered pre-filled returns without later legislation and funding.

Pre-filled returns work best for people whose income is fully reported to the IRS on W-2s and 1099s; taxpayers with unreported income, complex deductions, or business income would still need to file traditionally, and critics have long argued return-free filing could let errors or underreporting slide through unnoticed.
The required report contemplates delaying the start of the filing season so employers can submit wage data earlier, which could push back refunds for early filers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's substance was modest — a study and a stated goal — but it pointed at a change with real value for ordinary filers: reclaiming hours and preparation fees each spring. The main costs fall on a specific industry and on the IRS budget, not on taxpayers. The design was careful about privacy and choice, since it kept private software as an option. Its weakness is that it left the hard funding and legislative decisions to a future bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on April 4, 2017, joined by Sen. Elizabeth Warren.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The paid tax preparation and software industry kept the market for simple returns it would have risked losing, and no appropriations were required. Taxpayers with simple returns got no relief from filing costs or paperwork.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Paid tax preparers and software firms

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and asked Finance to consider IRS pre-prepared returns.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat without action until the Congress ended.

against.name: Intuit (maker of TurboTax)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for years against return-free filing proposals that would compete with its products.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and the Republican-led Finance Committee took no action on the bill; there is no recorded vote to measure broader party positions.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software companies (e.g. H&R Block, Intuit's TurboTax)
industries.note: Pre-filled IRS returns would let millions of simple-return filers skip paid preparation and software, cutting into a multi-billion-dollar seasonal market. The industry has historically lobbied against such proposals; the bill died in committee without a vote.

The IRS would gain new duties and need appropriations to build pre-filled filing, but would also simplify administration for wage earners whose income is already reported to it. The bill ordered a study of exactly these costs.
The bill's study contemplates earlier W-2 and 1099 deadlines and faster reporting so the IRS can pre-fill returns, which would move compliance work earlier in the year for businesses.
